original-en.context: Once upon a time there was a man who, as a child, had heard that beautiful tale of how God tempted Abraham, and how Abraham stood firm in the temptation, kept the faith, and a second time received a son against expectation. When he grew older, he read the same tale with still greater wonder; for life had divided what had been united in the child's pious simplicity. The older he grew, the more often his thought turned to that tale; his enthusiasm waxed stronger and stronger, and yet less and less could he understand the tale. At last he forgot all else for its sake; his soul had but one wish — to see Abraham — and one longing, to have been a witness of that event. His desire was not to behold the beautiful regions of the Orient, not the earthly glory of the promised land, not that god-fearing married couple whose old age God blessed, not the venerable figure of the aged patriarch, not the vigorous youth of Isaac whom God bestowed — he had nothing against its all taking place upon a barren heath. His craving was to accompany them on the three days' journey, when Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be present in the hour when Abraham lifted up his eye and saw the mountain of Moriah in the distance, the hour when he left the asses behind and went on alone with Isaac up to the mountain; for what occupied him was not the artistic weaving of the imagination, but the shudder of thought.

original-en.context: It was an early morning. Abraham rose betimes; he had the asses saddled, left his tent, and Isaac with him; but Sarah looked out of the window after them, down through the valley, until she saw them no more. They rode in silence for three days; on the morning of the fourth day Abraham still spoke not a word, but lifted up his eye and saw Mount Moriah in the distance. He left the lads behind and went on alone, with Isaac by the hand, up to the mountain. But Abraham said to himself: “I will not, however, conceal from Isaac whither this journey is leading him.” He stood still; he laid his hand upon Isaac's head in blessing, and Isaac bowed himself to receive it. And Abraham's countenance was that of a father, his glance was mild, his speech admonishing. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be uplifted; he clasped Abraham's knees, he made supplication at his foot, he pleaded for his young life, for his fair hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham's house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham raised the lad up and walked on with him by the hand, and his words were full of consolation and admonition. But Isaac could not understand him. He climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac understood him not. Then he turned away from him for a moment; but when Isaac the second time saw Abraham's countenance, it was changed: his glance was wild, his form was terror. He seized Isaac by the breast, he cast him to the ground, and said: “Foolish lad, believest thou that I am thy father? I am an idolater. Believest thou that this is God's command? No, it is my own pleasure.” Then Isaac trembled and cried out in his anguish: “God in heaven, have mercy upon me; God of Abraham, have mercy upon me; if I have no father upon earth, then be Thou my father!” But Abraham said softly within himself: “Lord in heaven, I thank Thee; it is, after all, better that he should believe me an inhuman wretch than that he should lose his faith in Thee.”

original-en.context: In our age, no man stops at faith, but every man goes further. To inquire whither they arrive would perhaps be a piece of audacity; on the other hand, it is surely a sign of breeding and culture that I assume every man has faith, since otherwise it would be a strange way of speaking — that he goes further. In those ancient days it was otherwise; then faith was a task for the whole of life, because it was assumed that the believing facility is not acquired in days nor in weeks. When, then, the seasoned old man drew near to his end, having fought the good fight and kept the faith, his heart was still young enough not to have forgotten that fear and trembling which chastened the youth, which the man indeed mastered, but from which no man wholly grows away — save in so far as he should succeed in going further as early as may be. Where those venerable figures arrived, in our age every man begins, in order to go further.

original-en.context: Were it not, after all, best to stop at faith, and is it not revolting that every man wisheth to go further? When in our age — and this is proclaimed in various ways — men will not stop at love, whither do they then come? To earthly cleverness, petty calculation, to wretchedness and misery, to all that can make man's divine origin doubtful. Were it not better that one stopped at faith, and that he who standeth take heed lest he fall; for the movement of faith must constantly be made by virtue of the absurd, yet, well to be marked, in such wise that one loseth not finitude, but winneth it whole and entire. I, for my part, can well describe the movements of faith, but I cannot make them. When one would learn the swimming-movements, then can one let oneself be hung in straps from the ceiling; one describeth indeed the movements, but one swimmeth not; thus can I describe the movements of faith, but when I am cast into the water I do indeed swim (for I am no wader), but I make other movements, I make the movements of infinity, while faith doeth the opposite — after having made the movements of infinity, it maketh those of finitude. Blessed be he who can make these movements; he doeth the marvelous, and I shall never grow weary of admiring him, whether it be Abraham, or it be the slave in Abraham's house, whether it be a professor of philosophy or a poor serving-maid, is to me absolutely indifferent; I look only upon the movements. But upon them I do also look, and I let myself be cheated neither by myself nor by any man. The knights of the infinite resignation are easily known; their gait is hovering, bold. They, on the other hand, who bear the treasure of faith, easily disappoint, because their outward bearing hath a striking resemblance to that which both the infinite resignation and faith deeply despise — to philistinism. I confess sincerely, in my practice I have not found any reliable specimen, without my for that reason wishing to deny that perhaps every other man is such a specimen. Meanwhile I have for several years sought it in vain. Men generally travel the world round to behold rivers and mountains, new stars, motley-feathered birds, mis-shapen fishes, ridiculous human races; one giveth oneself up to that brutish stupor that gapeth at existence, and supposeth that one hath seen something. This occupieth me not. Did I, however, know where such a knight of faith dwelt, then would I journey to him on foot; for this marvel occupieth me absolutely. I would not let him out of my sight a moment; every minute would I watch how he bore himself in the movements; I would account myself provided for in life, and divide my time betwixt looking upon him and exercising myself, and so spend all my time in admiring him. As I said, I have found no such one; meanwhile I can well think him. Here he is. The acquaintance is made; I am presented to him. The instant I first set my eyes upon him, I cast him from me again that same moment, take a leap backward, clap my hands together, and say half aloud: “Lord God! is this the man, is it really he? — he looketh just like a tax-collector.” Notwithstanding it is he. I draw a little nearer, watch the smallest movement, whether there should not show itself a little uneven fractional telegraphing from the infinite, a glance, a look, a gesture, a melancholy, a smile, that betrayed the infinite in its incongruity with the finite. No! I examine his figure from top to toe, whether there should not be a chink through which the infinite peeped out. No! He is solid through and through. His footing? It is firm, belongeth wholly to finitude; no spruce burgher who walketh out of a Sunday afternoon to Frederiksberg treadeth more solidly upon the earth; he belongeth wholly to the world, no philistine could belong to it more. Nothing is to be discovered of that strange and lofty nature whereby one knoweth the knight of the infinite. He delighteth himself in everything, taketh part in everything, and every time one seeth him take part in the particular, it is with a persistence which marketh the earthly man whose soul cleaveth fast unto such things. He goeth about his work. When one looketh upon him, one would think he were a clerk who had lost his soul in Italian book-keeping, so punctual is he. He keepeth holiday on Sunday. He goeth to church. No heavenly look, nor any sign of the incommensurable, betrayeth him; if one knew him not, it were impossible to single him out from the rest of the throng; for his sound, vigorous psalm-singing proveth at most that he hath a good chest. Of an afternoon he goeth to the wood. He rejoiceth over all that he seeth, over the throng of people, the new omnibuses, the Sound — when one meeteth him on the Strandvei, one would think he were some shopkeeper let loose; just so doth he enjoy himself; for he is no poet, and I have in vain sought to entice from him the poetic incommensurability. Toward evening he goeth home; his gait is unwearied as a postman's. On the way he thinketh that his wife hath surely some special little warm dish for him,

original-en.context: Upon this peak standeth Abraham. The last stage which he loseth from sight is the infinite resignation. He goeth in truth further and cometh to faith; for all those caricatures of faith, the wretched lukewarm sluggishness which thinketh: there is no danger, it is not worth grieving before the time; the miserable hope which saith: one cannot know what shall happen, it might still be possible — these caricatures belong at home in the wretchedness of life, and them already the infinite resignation hath infinitely despised.

He really goes further and arrives at faith; for all those caricatures of faith — the wretched lukewarm sloth that thinks: there is probably no danger, it is not worth grieving before the time; the miserable hope that says: one cannot know what will happen, it is at least possible — these caricatures belong in life's wretchedness, and infinite resignation has already infinitely despised them.

original-en.context: The present author is by no means a philosopher; he has not comprehended the System — whether it exists, whether it is finished. He already has enough to do for his weak head with the thought of what a prodigious head every man in our age must have, since every man has such a prodigious thought. Even were one able to transpose the entire content of faith into the form of the concept, it would not follow that one had comprehended faith — comprehended how one came into it, or how it came into one. The present author is by no means a philosopher; he is, poetice et eleganter, a supplementary scribe, who neither writes the System nor promises of the System, who neither subscribes himself to the System nor signs himself over to it. He writes because for him it is a luxury, which gains in agreeableness and self-evidence the fewer there are who buy and read what he writes. He readily foresees his fate in an age that has drawn a line through passion in order to serve science — an age in which an author who would have readers must take care so to write that his book may conveniently be leafed through during the after-dinner nap, and take care to model his outward bearing after that polite gardener's apprentice in the Adresseavisen who, hat in hand and with good recommendations from the place where he last served, recommends himself to a most honored public. He foresees his fate, to be wholly ignored; he divines the more dreadful prospect that the zealous criticism will several times stand him at the school-bench; he shudders at the still more dreadful prospect that some industrious registrar, some paragraph-glutton (who, to save science, is always ready to do unto the writings of others what Trop, “to save taste,” magnanimously did unto The Destruction of the Human Race) will cut him up into §§, and do it with the same inflexibility as that man who, to serve the science of punctuation, divided his discourse by counting the words, so that fifty words made one full stop and thirty-five a semicolon. — I prostrate myself in deepest humility before every systematic peeping-Tom: “This is not the System; it has not the slightest thing to do with the System. I call down every blessing upon the System and upon the Danish shareholders in this Omnibus — for a tower, indeed, it will scarcely become. I wish them all and every one of them luck and benediction.”
